title: C++ Developer Plan

about.label: The goal
about.text: Not 'know C++'. The goal: someone gives you a problem you've never seen, and you know how to figure it out.

about.label: The mindset
about.text: "I don't know how to do this YET. I'll investigate, break it down, experiment, and figure it out."

about.label: Time
about.text: 30-60 minutes a session, about 5 sessions a week. Sessions are numbered, not tied to days. Missed a day? Just carry on with the next one.

milestones.bigQuestion: How do I turn a real-world problem into a program?
milestones.outcome: A console program with a menu that adds and lists students.

milestones.bigQuestion: How does a program find, change and remove things?
What happens when users do something unexpected?
milestones.outcome: An app that bad input can't break, and you can use a debugger.

milestones.bigQuestion: How does a program remember things after it closes?
milestones.outcome: Save/load to a file, and a plan for splitting up your code.
Code split into files and classes, plus your first automatic tests.

milestones.bigQuestion: Can I change the screen without touching the logic?
milestones.outcome: A Qt window running on the same logic. Project 1 done!

milestones.bigQuestion: How do different kinds of data connect?
milestones.outcome: Books, members and borrowing with rules.

milestones.bigQuestion: How do I handle things that are similar but not the same?
milestones.outcome: Waitlists, books AND DVDs, saving linked data, tests. Project 2 done!

milestones.bigQuestion: How do I turn many records into useful answers?
milestones.outcome: Expenses with sorting, filtering and totals. Project 3 done!

milestones.bigQuestion: How do I solve a problem nobody has taught me?
milestones.outcome: A small search engine you researched and designed yourself.

milestones.bigQuestion: Can I plan a project myself?
milestones.outcome: Your own app idea, scoped, designed and half built.

milestones.bigQuestion: Can I finish, test and explain it?
milestones.outcome: A finished app you can demo and explain.

tasks.title: Understand the problem, then build a menu

steps.text: Create requirements.txt. Describe the 5 features (add, view, search, update, delete) in YOUR OWN words.
For each feature write: what the user gives the program (input) and what they get back (output).
Create a new C++ console project called StudentManager.
Make it show a numbered menu (1 Add, 2 View all, 3 Search, 4 Update, 5 Delete, 0 Exit), read the choice and print 'You chose: Add' etc.
Show the menu again after each choice, until the user picks 0.
draw the menu screens on paper first.

thinkAbout: What's the difference between WHAT a program must do and HOW it does it?
Which kind of loop fits 'keep going until the user says stop'?

doneWhen.text: requirements.txt has 5 features, each with input + output.
The menu keeps coming back until you pick 0.
Check: every option; a number that isn't on the menu (like 7).

tasks.title: Describe a student in code

steps.text: A student has: ID, name, age, major, GPA. For each, decide what kind of value it is - whole number, decimal or text? Write your reasons in requirements.txt.
Create your own Student type that groups these 5 values together.
When the user picks 'Add', ask for each value, fill in a Student, and print it back neatly.
write a function that turns a Student into one neat line of text.

thinkAbout: Why is age a whole number but GPA a decimal?
Type a name with a space (e.g. 'Priya Sharma'). What happens? Why?

doneWhen.text: Add asks for all 5 values and prints them back correctly.
Check: a name with a space; GPA 0 and 4; a long major name.

tasks.title: Remember many students
intro: Right now the program forgets a student as soon as you add the next one.

steps.text: Find a way to keep a LIST of students that grows each time you add someone. (Look up 'vector' in the Concepts tab.)
'Add' puts the new student into the list.
'View all' prints every student, one per line.
If there are no students, 'View all' says 'No students yet.'
print the students as a neat table with lined-up columns.

thinkAbout: Why not just make 100 separate Student variables?
How do you go through every item in a list, one by one?

doneWhen.text: Add 5 students; View all shows all 5 in the order added.
View all with no students shows the friendly message.

tasks.title: Split main() into functions
intro: Your main() is getting long and hard to read.

steps.text: List the separate jobs main() does (show menu, add a student, print all...).
Move each job into its own function with a clear name, e.g. addStudent, printAllStudents.
main() should become short: show menu, read choice, call the right function.
Some functions need the student list. Find out how to give them the list WITHOUT making a copy.
no function longer than 20 lines.

thinkAbout: What makes a good function name?
If addStudent gets a COPY of the list, what happens to the student you add?

doneWhen.text: main() fits on one screen.
Each function does one job and its name says what.
Add and View all still work exactly as before.

tasks.title: Find a student by ID
intro: PSEUDOCODE FIRST: write the steps in Notes using the template on Start Here.

steps.text: Add a menu option 'Search by ID'.
Write a function that looks through the list and gives back WHERE the student is (their position), or a special value meaning 'not found'.
Print the student, or 'No student with ID 105'.
count how many students your search checked, and print it.

thinkAbout: With 1 million students, how many would you check in the worst case?
What should the function give back when nothing is found?

doneWhen.text: Pseudocode is in Notes (written BEFORE the code).
Check: first student, last student, an ID that doesn't exist, an empty list.

tasks.title: Search by part of a name

steps.text: Split this into two smaller problems: (a) make upper/lower case not matter, (b) check whether one piece of text contains another.
Solve each small problem in its own function. Test each one alone.
Combine them: print EVERY student whose name matches.
search the major too.

thinkAbout: How can 'Pri' and 'pri' be compared as equal?
How do you check if one string contains another in C++?

doneWhen.text: Shows all matches, not just the first.
Check: 'PRI', 'pri', a letter from the middle of a name, no matches, empty search.

tasks.title: Update a student

steps.text: Ask for an ID and find the student (reuse your search function!).
Show their current details, then ask for new values.
Save the changes into the list.
If 'View all' still shows the OLD values, stop and investigate: are you changing the real student, or a copy?
pressing Enter without typing keeps the old value.

thinkAbout: What's the difference between  Student s = list[i];  and  Student& s = list[i];  ?

doneWhen.text: Changes show up in View all.
In Notes, explain copy vs reference in your own words.
Check: update an ID that doesn't exist; change every field.

tasks.title: Delete a student

steps.text: Ask for an ID and find the student.
Ask 'Are you sure? (y/n)'.
Remove them from the list.
Before running it, predict: after deleting the 2nd of 4 students, what position is the old 3rd student in now?
'Delete all students' with a double confirmation.

thinkAbout: How do you remove an item from the middle of a vector?
Why is 'delete student ID 105' safer than 'delete the 3rd student'?

doneWhen.text: The right student is removed.
Check: first, last and middle student; missing ID; answering 'n'; deleting the only student.

tasks.title: Try to break your own app (no coding today!)
intro: Be a user who makes mistakes - or who is trying to break things.

steps.text: Use the 7 test types on the Start Here tab.
Try at least 15 things. For each, write in bugs.txt: what I did -> what happened -> what SHOULD happen.

Don't fix anything today. Just collect.
Must try: typing a letter when it asks for age.
rank the 3 bugs a real user would hate most.

thinkAbout: What does 'boundary value' mean for GPA (0.0 to 4.0)? Which exact values should you try?

doneWhen.text: bugs.txt has 15+ entries, each with: steps, what happened, what should happen.

tasks.title: Read numbers safely
intro: You probably found that typing letters where a number is expected breaks the program badly.

steps.text: Research WHY that happens.
Write ONE helper function that asks a question and keeps asking until the user types a valid whole number in a range, e.g.  readInt("Age: ", 16, 100).
Make similar helpers for decimals (GPA) and for non-empty text (name).
Use these helpers everywhere you read input, including the menu.
reject '12abc' and '3.5' when a whole number is expected.

thinkAbout: What happens to std::cin when it can't read a number?
What does std::stoi do when given 'abc'?

doneWhen.text: No input can crash or freeze the app.
Check: letters, empty, -5, 999, 3.5 for age, only spaces.
Mark the fixed bugs in bugs.txt.

tasks.title: Rules: valid students and unique IDs
intro: Some rules aren't about typing, they're about the data itself.

steps.text: Write every rule for a valid student (e.g. name not blank, GPA 0-4, ID not already used).
Write ONE function that checks a student against all rules and returns a message saying what's wrong (or nothing if it's fine).
Use it in both Add and Update.
Careful with Update: a student keeping their OWN ID is fine.
show ALL problems at once, not just the first.

thinkAbout: Why keep all the rules in one function instead of checking separately in Add and Update?
Why is 'update student 101 but keep ID 101' a tricky case?

doneWhen.text: Duplicate IDs are impossible.
Check: add a duplicate ID (fails); update keeping own ID (works); update to another student's ID (fails); update to a new free ID (works).

tasks.title: Use the debugger
intro: Print statements only get you so far. A debugger lets you pause the program and look inside.

steps.text: Find how to set a breakpoint (in Qt Creator: click left of a line number).
Put one in your search function. Run in Debug mode.
Step through line by line. Watch the variables change.
Ask your mentor for a 'mystery bug' (or pick one from bugs.txt) and find it using ONLY the debugger.
use the call stack to see which function called which.

thinkAbout: What's the difference between 'Step Over' and 'Step Into'?
What does the call stack show?

doneWhen.text: You found a bug using breakpoints and stepping.
In Notes: what you expected, what you saw, what the cause was.

steps.text: Anything this week not 'Done'? Finish that first.

Every bugs.txt entry is marked.

tasks.title: Design how to save students (no coding)
intro: When the program closes, every student is lost. You'll fix that by saving to a file. Today, design only:

steps.text: By hand, write 2 students into students.txt in a layout you like (e.g. one student per line).
What separates the values? What if a name contains that character?
When do you save: after every change, or on Exit? When do you load?
Write your choices and reasons in design_storage.txt.

thinkAbout: What is a CSV file? What goes wrong with the name 'Smith, John' in a CSV?
What's the risk of only saving on Exit?

doneWhen.text: design_storage.txt explains your format and when you save/load, with reasons.
A hand-written students.txt exists.

tasks.title: Save students to a file

steps.text: Save all students into a file using your format.
Plan your own steps in Notes first.
Rule: if the file can't be opened, tell the user. Never fail silently.
save to a temporary file first, then rename it - so a crash can't leave a half-written file.

thinkAbout: How do you write to a file in C++?
How do you know if opening the file failed?
When does the file get closed? (Look up RAII.)

doneWhen.text: Open the file in a text editor: every student is there and correct.
Check: 0 students, 10 students, a name containing your separator character.

tasks.title: Load students from the file

steps.text: When the program starts, load the students back.
Before coding, think about bad cases: no file yet (first run), a line with missing values, age written as 'abc', a duplicate ID in the file.
Plan your own steps.

thinkAbout: How do you split one line of text into pieces in C++?
Should one bad line stop ALL students from loading?
Can you reuse your rules function from week 3?

doneWhen.text: Close and reopen: your data is back.
Check: first run with no file; hand-edit the file to break a line in each of the ways above. Clear message, no crash.

tasks.title: Audit: what is main.cpp doing?

steps.text: Count the lines in main.cpp.
List EVERY job it does: showing menus, reading input, checking rules, searching, saving files...

Sort the jobs into 4 boxes:
- Screen (talking to the user)
- Rules (what's allowed)
- Data (what a student is)
- Storage (files)
Draw the boxes with arrows showing who uses whom. Save as architecture.txt or a photo.

thinkAbout: If you wanted a WINDOW app instead of a console app, which of your code could stay exactly the same?
If you switched from a text file to a database, which code would change?

doneWhen.text: Every function is in a box. The drawing is done.
You can explain in 2 sentences why the boxes exist.

tasks.title: Move Student into its own files
intro: Create Student.h and Student.cpp and move the Student type into them.

steps.text: Find out what belongs in a .h file and what belongs in a .cpp file.
Tell the build system about the new files (CMakeLists.txt).

Fix compile errors one at a time, starting from the TOP of the list.
The program must behave exactly the same as before.

thinkAbout: Why do C++ projects split code into .h and .cpp files?
What does #pragma once prevent?

doneWhen.text: Student lives in its own files.
Regression check: run everything in bugs.txt - all still behaves the same.

tasks.title: Turn the rules into a StudentService class
intro: Create a class StudentService that OWNS the student list and offers: add, update, remove, findById, searchByName.

steps.text: The list is private: only the service can change it.
Your rules function moves in too.
The service must NEVER print or read from the console. It returns results and error messages instead.
main.cpp now asks the service to do things.

thinkAbout: Why make the list private?
If the service can't print, how does it tell main.cpp that something went wrong?

doneWhen.text: No rules or searching left in main.cpp.
StudentService.cpp contains no std::cout or std::cin.
Everything works as before.

tasks.title: Move saving/loading into StudentStorage

steps.text: Create StudentStorage with save and load. Then organize folders:
models/ (Student)   services/ (StudentService)   storage/ (StudentStorage)   ui/ (the console menu)
You decide: who calls storage - the menu or the service? Write down why.

thinkAbout: Who should decide WHEN to save, and who should decide HOW?

doneWhen.text: 4 folders, each with the right files. main.cpp is short.
Everything works, including save and load.

tasks.title: Prove it: test the rules without the menu
intro: Because the rules no longer need the console, you can test them automatically.

steps.text: Create a second small program, tests.cpp, that uses StudentService directly - no menu.
Write at least 8 checks, e.g. 'adding a duplicate ID is rejected', 'searching pri finds Priya'. Print PASS or FAIL for each.
Break a rule on purpose inside StudentService. Does a test catch it?

thinkAbout: What is a unit test?
How do you add a second program (executable) in CMakeLists.txt?

doneWhen.text: 8+ checks run in one go and all pass.
A deliberate bug was caught by a test.

tasks.title: Put a window on top of your logic
intro: Time to use your Qt skills. Create a Qt Widgets project that uses your models/, services/ and storage/ folders UNCHANGED.

steps.text: Show a window with a table of all students loaded from your file.
Rule for this week: only edit files in ui/. If you must change anything else, write down why in Notes.

thinkAbout: How can a Qt project use source files from other folders?
In a console app YOU control the order of things. Who controls it in a window app?

doneWhen.text: The window shows the students from your saved file.
No files outside ui/ changed (or each change is explained).

tasks.title: Add students from the window

steps.text: A form (ID, name, age, major, GPA) and an Add button.
Show the service's error messages in a message box. Refresh the table after each add.

thinkAbout: Where should the error message text come from - the window or the service? Why?

doneWhen.text: Adding works, and every rule from week 3 applies without being rewritten.

tasks.title: Search, update and delete in the window

steps.text: Bring the other 3 features to the window. Selecting a row should fill the form for editing.

thinkAbout: If the table is filtered by a search, does row 2 still mean the 3rd student in the list?

doneWhen.text: All 5 features work in the window.
Check: delete while a search filter is showing - is the RIGHT student deleted?

tasks.title: Compare: one brain, two faces
intro: Your console app and your window app now run on the SAME logic.

steps.text: Run tests.cpp - still passing?
Count how many lines you changed outside ui/ this week.
Write a short note: what would have happened if you'd built the window app in week 1 with all the logic inside the window?

thinkAbout: Where do real companies do this? (Think of a bank with a website AND a phone app.)

doneWhen.text: Both apps work. Tests pass. Note written.

tasks.title: Library: requirements and data design
intro: A small library lends books to members.
Requirements: add books (ID, title, author) and members (ID, name). Members borrow and return books. A member can have at most 3 books. The app shows who has what.

steps.text: List the kinds of things (entities) and their information.
Draw how they connect. A borrowing (a 'loan') links a book and a member.
Decide: should a loan store the book's ID, or a pointer to the book? Research both, write your decision.
Decide: console or Qt? Your call.

thinkAbout: What is a pointer? What happens to a pointer to an item in a vector when the vector grows?
Can you save a pointer into a file and load it back?

doneWhen.text: design.txt with entities, a drawing, and the IDs-vs-pointers decision with reasons.

tasks.title: Library: set up, books and members

steps.text: Start with the 4 folders from day 1 (models, services, storage, ui). Add and list books and members, with rules (no duplicate IDs, no blank names).
Plan your own steps.

thinkAbout: What did you do in the Student Manager that you'd do differently now?

doneWhen.text: Books and members can be added and listed, with rules. The structure is in place.

tasks.title: Library: borrow a book

steps.text: Requirement: a member borrows an available book.
Rules: the book exists and isn't already out; the member exists; max 3 books at once.
PSEUDOCODE FIRST. Check EVERY rule before changing anything.
Decide: does a book remember 'I'm borrowed', or do you work it out from the loans? What if those two ever disagree?

thinkAbout: What is 'state' in a program?
What can go wrong when the same fact is stored in two places?

doneWhen.text: Check: borrow an available book; a book already out; a 4th book; unknown member; unknown book.

tasks.title: Library: returns, history and overdue

steps.text: Requirement: members return books. Keep old loans as history. Show overdue loans. A loan lasts 14 days.
Real dates are complicated, so SIMPLIFY: the app keeps a 'today' day number (starting at 1), and a menu option 'Next day' moves time forward. A loan is overdue if today > due day.

thinkAbout: Why is a fake 'today' easier to test than the real clock?
Why keep returned loans instead of deleting them?

doneWhen.text: Check: return a borrowed book; return one that isn't borrowed; borrow on day 1, then check overdue on day 15 and day 16.

tasks.title: Library: waitlist

steps.text: Requirement: if a book is out, members can join its waitlist. When it's returned, it goes to the first person in line.
Research which container fits 'first come, first served', and how to keep one line per book.

thinkAbout: What does FIFO mean?
How would you keep a separate line for EACH book?

doneWhen.text: Check: 3 people wait for one book (order kept); the same person joins twice; someone joins the waitlist for a book that's available.

tasks.title: Library: DVDs too (similar, not the same)

steps.text: Requirement: the library also lends DVDs. Books are loaned for 14 days, DVDs for 7. Both have an ID and title; books have an author, DVDs have a running time.
Treat them the same where they're the same (borrow, return, list) and differently where they differ - WITHOUT 'if it's a DVD... else...' scattered everywhere.

thinkAbout: What is inheritance? What is a virtual function?
Why can't a plain vector<Item> hold books and DVDs properly? (Search 'object slicing'.)
What is std::unique_ptr?

doneWhen.text: One list holds both books and DVDs. Borrowing uses the right loan length.
Adding a 3rd type (e.g. Magazine) wouldn't change the borrowing code.

tasks.title: Library: save and load everything

steps.text: Requirement: books, DVDs, members, loans, waitlists and 'today' all survive a restart. A member who still has items can't be deleted.

thinkAbout: How do you record 'this is a DVD, not a book' in a text file?
What should happen if the file has a loan for item 99 but item 99 doesn't exist?

doneWhen.text: Everything survives a restart.
Check: hand-edit the file to break a link - the app warns instead of crashing.

tasks.title: Library: tests for the rules

steps.text: Write automatic tests (like week 5) for the borrowing rules: max 3 items, can't borrow twice, waitlist order, DVDs last 7 days, overdue on the right day.

thinkAbout: Which of these are boundary cases? (3rd vs 4th item, day 14 vs day 15...)

doneWhen.text: 10+ tests pass. One deliberate bug was caught.

tasks.title: Expenses: design, and why money is tricky
intro: Requirements: record expenses (date, amount, category, description); list, delete, save; sort; filter; totals per category and per month.

steps.text: Design the data and the folders/classes - you know how now.
Before choosing a type for 'amount', try this: add 0.1 + 0.2 as doubles and print the result with 17 digits. Research what you see.

thinkAbout: Why don't banks store money as decimals? What do they store instead?
How could you store dates so they sort correctly as text? (Hint: YYYY-MM-DD.)

doneWhen.text: design.txt with the data, the structure, and your money-type decision explained.

tasks.title: Expenses: the core

steps.text: Add, list, delete and save expenses, with rules. This should feel fast - it's your third time.
undo the last add or delete (research 'stack' in the Concepts tab).

thinkAbout: What did you copy from earlier projects? What did you improve?

doneWhen.text: Core works.
Check: amount 0, negative, 12.345, empty category.

tasks.title: Expenses: sort and filter

steps.text: Requirement: sort by date or by amount (both directions); filter by category and by a date range.
Use the standard library's sort, and tell it HOW to compare using a lambda.

thinkAbout: What is a lambda? What does the [ ] part (capture) mean?
What must a sort comparison return?

doneWhen.text: Check: empty list; equal amounts; start date after end date; a category with no expenses.

tasks.title: Expenses: totals

steps.text: Requirement: total per category for a chosen month, and total per month.
Research which container maps a category name to a running total.

thinkAbout: map vs unordered_map: which keeps keys in order? Which suits a report?
What does std::accumulate do?

doneWhen.text: Totals match a hand calculation for one month.

tasks.title: Research: how does search find things fast?
intro: You have NOT been taught this - that's the point.

steps.text: Research how a search engine finds documents containing a word quickly.
In research.txt, explain it in your own words with a tiny example you work out by hand (3 short sentences as 'documents').

Collect 20-50 .txt files to search (e.g. short stories).

concepts.name: Requirements
concepts.plain: A clear list of what the program must do, from the user's point of view.
concepts.example: A shopping list says 'milk', not 'drive down Main St to the store'.
concepts.why: If you don't know exactly what to build, you'll build the wrong thing.

concepts.name: Console program
concepts.plain: A text-only program: it prints text and reads what you type.
concepts.example: Texting back and forth with the program.
concepts.why: Lets you focus on logic without designing screens.

concepts.name: Loop
concepts.plain: Repeating code while something is true, or once for each item in a list.
concepts.example: Keep stirring until the sauce thickens.
concepts.why: Almost every program repeats something.

concepts.name: Condition
concepts.plain: Running code only if a test is true (if / else / switch).
concepts.example: If it's raining, take an umbrella.
concepts.why: Programs make decisions.

concepts.name: Data model
concepts.plain: Deciding what information your program stores, and what kind each piece is.
concepts.example: A contact card: name (text), phone (digits), birthday (date).
concepts.why: Bad data design makes every later feature harder.

concepts.name: Variable & type
concepts.plain: A named box holding a value. The type says what kind: whole number (int), decimal (double), text (string)...
concepts.example: Labelled jars: you don't pour milk into the sugar jar.
concepts.why: The right type prevents whole groups of bugs.

concepts.name: struct
concepts.plain: Your own type that groups related values together under one name.
concepts.example: A form with fields: name, age, major.
concepts.why: Keeps related data together instead of loose variables.

concepts.name: std::string
concepts.plain: C++'s type for text.
concepts.example: A line of writing.
concepts.why: Names, messages, file contents - most programs handle lots of text.

concepts.name: Compiler error
concepts.plain: The compiler telling you your code isn't valid C++. Always read the FIRST error first.
concepts.example: A spell-checker underlining a word.
concepts.why: The first error often causes the rest. Reading errors calmly is a core skill.

concepts.name: Single source of truth
concepts.plain: Keep each fact in exactly ONE place; everything else reads from there.
concepts.example: One shared family calendar instead of everyone keeping their own copy.
concepts.why: Two copies of a fact eventually disagree - and that's a bug.

concepts.name: vector
concepts.plain: A list that grows as you add items and keeps them in order. Written std::vector<Student>.
concepts.example: A notebook where you can keep adding pages.
concepts.why: The go-to C++ container for 'many of something'.

concepts.name: Breaking a problem down
concepts.plain: Splitting a big problem into small problems you can solve one at a time.
concepts.example: 'Cook dinner' -> buy food, chop, cook, serve.
concepts.why: Every hard problem is a pile of easy ones.

concepts.name: Function
concepts.plain: A named block of code that does one job. You can use (call) it whenever you need that job done.
concepts.example: The 'make coffee' button on a machine.
concepts.why: Good names make code readable; one job per function makes it fixable.

concepts.name: Reference vs copy
concepts.plain: A copy is a separate duplicate. A reference (&) is another name for the original.
concepts.example: A photocopy of a document vs the original document.
concepts.why: Change a copy and the original doesn't change - a very common bug.

concepts.name: Regression test
concepts.plain: Re-testing old features to make sure new changes didn't break them.
concepts.example: After fixing a car's brakes, checking the lights still work.
concepts.why: New code often breaks old code.

concepts.name: Pseudocode
concepts.plain: Writing the steps in plain English before writing code.
concepts.example: Writing down a recipe before you start cooking.
concepts.why: Fixing a mistake in your plan is much cheaper than fixing it in code.

concepts.name: Algorithm
concepts.plain: A precise, step-by-step method for solving a problem.
concepts.example: The way you look up a word in a paper dictionary.
concepts.why: Code is just an algorithm written for a computer.

concepts.name: Linear search
concepts.plain: Checking items one by one until you find the one you want.
concepts.example: Checking every pocket for your keys.
concepts.why: Simple and fine for small lists; slow for huge ones.

concepts.name: Big-O
concepts.plain: A way to describe how work grows as data grows. O(n): double the data, double the work. O(1): same work no matter what.
concepts.example: Reading every name in a phone book (O(n)) vs jumping straight to the right page.
concepts.why: Tells you whether your program survives 1000x more data.

concepts.name: DRY
concepts.plain: 'Don't Repeat Yourself': write a piece of logic once and reuse it.
concepts.example: Using a stamp instead of hand-drawing a logo every time.
concepts.why: Repeated code gets fixed in one place and forgotten in the others.

concepts.name: ID vs position
concepts.plain: Identify things by a permanent ID, not by where they sit in a list.
concepts.example: Your student ID vs 'the 3rd person in line' - the line keeps changing.
concepts.why: Positions shift when items are added or removed; IDs don't.

concepts.name: Edge case
concepts.plain: An unusual situation at the limits: empty, first, last, huge, missing.
concepts.example: Pressing a vending machine button without inserting money.
concepts.why: Most bugs hide at the edges.

concepts.name: Documentation
concepts.plain: Writing that explains what the program does, how to run it, and why it's built this way.
concepts.example: An instruction manual.
concepts.why: Future you - and teammates - will need it.
concepts.learnMore: Search: 'how to write a good README'

concepts.name: Testing
concepts.plain: Deliberately trying things to find where the program is wrong.
concepts.example: Test-driving a car before buying it.
concepts.why: If you don't find your bugs, your users will.
concepts.learnMore: See Start Here: the 7 test types

concepts.name: Boundary value
concepts.plain: The exact values at a rule's limit. For GPA 0-4: test -0.1, 0, 4 and 4.1.
concepts.example: A ride's height limit: test someone exactly at the line.
concepts.why: 'Off by one' mistakes live here.

concepts.name: Bug report
concepts.plain: A note saying: what I did, what happened, what should have happened.
concepts.example: Telling a mechanic exactly what noise and when.
concepts.why: A clear report is half the fix.

concepts.name: Exception
concepts.plain: A way for code to signal 'something went wrong' that must be handled (try / catch).
concepts.example: A fire alarm: normal work stops until someone deals with it.
concepts.why: Some errors can't safely be ignored.

concepts.name: Input validation
concepts.plain: Checking input before using it, and rejecting bad values with a clear message.
concepts.example: A form that won't accept letters in a phone number.
concepts.why: Never trust input: people make mistakes.

concepts.name: Business rules
concepts.plain: Rules about what's allowed in the real-world problem (not about code).
concepts.example: A library: max 3 books per member.
concepts.why: Rules must live in one place, or some path will skip them.

concepts.name: const
concepts.plain: A promise that something won't be changed. The compiler enforces it.
concepts.example: 'Read-only' on a shared document.
concepts.why: Stops accidental changes before they happen.

concepts.name: Debugging
concepts.plain: Finding a bug by guessing a cause, testing the guess, and repeating.
concepts.example: A doctor: symptom -> likely cause -> test.
concepts.why: Random changes waste hours; testing guesses finds bugs.

concepts.name: Debugger
concepts.plain: A tool that pauses your program at a line (breakpoint) so you can inspect variables and step through line by line.
concepts.example: Pausing and slow-motion replaying a video.
concepts.why: Much faster than print statements for tricky bugs.

concepts.name: Tradeoff
concepts.plain: Every choice gives you something and costs you something.
concepts.example: A car is faster than a bike but costs more to run.
concepts.why: Engineers choose on purpose and can explain why.

concepts.name: Persistence
concepts.plain: Keeping data after the program closes, usually in files or a database.
concepts.example: Saving a game.
concepts.why: Almost every real app remembers things.

concepts.name: File format
concepts.plain: The agreed layout of data inside a file (e.g. CSV: values separated by commas).
concepts.example: A paper form everyone fills in the same way.
concepts.why: Saving and loading must agree exactly on the format.

concepts.name: File I/O
concepts.plain: Reading from and writing to files (ifstream / ofstream).
concepts.example: Writing in a notebook and reading it later.
concepts.why: Without it, everything is forgotten when the program closes.

concepts.name: RAII
concepts.plain: Resources (files, memory) are released automatically when the object that owns them goes away.
concepts.example: A hotel key card that stops working at checkout without you doing anything.
concepts.why: No forgotten clean-up = fewer leaks and bugs.

concepts.name: Fail loudly
concepts.plain: When something goes wrong, say so clearly - never silently carry on.
concepts.example: A smoke alarm that beeps rather than staying quiet.
concepts.why: Silent failures turn into mystery bugs later.

concepts.name: Parsing
concepts.plain: Turning raw text into structured data.
concepts.example: Reading '12/05/2026' and knowing which part is day, month and year.
concepts.why: Files and user input always arrive as text.

concepts.name: Trust boundary
concepts.plain: Any place data comes in from outside (user, file, network). Check it there.
concepts.example: Airport security at the entrance, not in every room.
concepts.why: Files can be edited or broken - treat them like user input.

concepts.name: Separation of concerns
concepts.plain: Each part of the program handles one kind of job.
concepts.example: In a restaurant, waiters don't cook and chefs don't take orders.
concepts.why: You can change one part without breaking the others.

concepts.name: Layers
concepts.plain: Organizing code as Screen -> Rules -> Data -> Storage, each part only talking to its neighbour.
concepts.example: Restaurant: dining room -> kitchen -> pantry.
concepts.why: Swap the screen (console -> window) or storage (file -> database) without rewriting the rest.

concepts.name: Coupling & cohesion
concepts.plain: Coupling = how much parts depend on each other (want LOW). Cohesion = how well a part's contents belong together (want HIGH).
concepts.example: A toolbox with one drawer per tool type (high cohesion) that opens without needing the car keys (low coupling).
concepts.why: Low coupling + high cohesion = code that's easy to change.

concepts.name: Refactoring
concepts.plain: Improving the structure of code without changing what it does.
concepts.example: Reorganizing a closet: same clothes, easier to find.
concepts.why: Code gets messy as it grows; refactoring keeps it workable.

concepts.name: Header & source files
concepts.plain: .h files say WHAT exists; .cpp files say HOW it works.
concepts.example: A restaurant menu (.h) vs the kitchen's recipes (.cpp).
concepts.why: Real programs have many files; other files only need to see the 'menu'.

concepts.name: Build system (CMake)
concepts.plain: The file (CMakeLists.txt) that tells the compiler which files make up your program.
concepts.example: The ingredients list of a recipe.
concepts.why: Every real project has one; new files must be added to it.

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.plain: Hiding an object's data so only its own functions can change it.
concepts.example: You use an ATM's buttons; you can't reach inside for the cash.
concepts.why: Rules can't be skipped if nobody can touch the data directly.

concepts.name: class
concepts.plain: Like a struct, but bundles data WITH the functions that work on it, and can hide its data (private).
concepts.example: A microwave: its insides plus the buttons you're allowed to press.
concepts.why: Lets you build parts with clear jobs and protected data.

concepts.name: Constructor
concepts.plain: A special function that runs when an object is created, to set it up correctly.
concepts.example: Filling in the form when you open a bank account.
concepts.why: Objects start life in a valid state.

concepts.name: Unit test
concepts.plain: A small automatic check that one piece of logic gives the right answer.
concepts.example: A pilot's pre-flight checklist.
concepts.why: Re-check everything in seconds after any change.

concepts.name: GUI & events
concepts.plain: A window program waits for the user to do something (click, type) and reacts to it.
concepts.example: A doorbell: nothing happens until someone presses it.
concepts.why: Most apps you use every day work this way.

concepts.name: Architecture
concepts.plain: The overall plan of a program's parts and how they fit together.
concepts.example: A building's floor plan.
concepts.why: Good architecture makes new features easy; bad makes everything hard.

concepts.name: Relationships between data
concepts.plain: How different kinds of data connect, e.g. 'a member has many loans'.
concepts.example: A class list links students to courses.
concepts.why: Real problems are rarely one list; they're connected things.

concepts.name: Pointer
concepts.plain: A variable that holds the memory ADDRESS of something, rather than the thing itself.
concepts.example: A note saying 'the book is on shelf 3' instead of the book.
concepts.why: Powerful but risky: if the thing moves, the note is wrong.

concepts.name: Stack vs heap memory
concepts.plain: Stack: fast, automatic memory for local variables. Heap: memory you ask for, which lives until released.
concepts.example: Stack: sticky notes on your desk. Heap: a storage unit you rent.
concepts.why: Explains object lifetimes, pointers and memory leaks.

concepts.name: State
concepts.plain: What the program currently remembers, which affects what it does next.
concepts.example: A traffic light: what happens next depends on its current colour.
concepts.why: Many bugs are state that's wrong or out of sync.

concepts.name: Simplifying a problem
concepts.plain: Replacing a hard part with a simpler version so you can make progress.
concepts.example: Practising a song slowly before playing it at full speed.
concepts.why: Make it work first; make it realistic later.

concepts.name: queue
concepts.plain: A line: first in, first out (FIFO).
concepts.example: The line at a coffee shop.
concepts.why: Use when order of arrival matters.

concepts.name: map
concepts.plain: Stores pairs of key -> value; look things up by key. Keeps keys sorted.
concepts.example: A dictionary: word -> meaning.
concepts.why: Fast lookup by name or ID, and sorted output for reports.

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.plain: Making a new class based on an existing one: a DVD IS AN Item.
concepts.example: Cars and bikes are both vehicles.
concepts.why: Share what's common, write only what's different.

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.plain: Different types answering the same question in their own way (virtual functions).
concepts.example: 'Make a sound': a dog barks, a cat meows.
concepts.why: Add new types without changing the code that uses them.

concepts.name: Smart pointer (unique_ptr)
concepts.plain: A pointer that automatically frees what it points to when no longer needed.
concepts.example: A library book that returns itself when you're done.
concepts.why: Heap memory without manual delete or leaks.

concepts.name: Data integrity
concepts.plain: Data stays correct and consistent - e.g. no loans for books that don't exist.
concepts.example: A library card for a person who doesn't exist is useless.
concepts.why: Broken data breaks everything built on top of it.

concepts.name: Floating-point numbers
concepts.plain: double/float store decimals APPROXIMATELY, not exactly.
concepts.example: Writing 1/3 as 0.333 - close, but not exact.
concepts.why: Money needs exact values: store whole cents instead.

concepts.name: stack
concepts.plain: A pile: last in, first out (LIFO).
concepts.example: A stack of plates.
concepts.why: Undo buttons work like this - so do function calls.

concepts.name: Lambda
concepts.plain: A small unnamed function written right where you need it.
concepts.example: A sticky note 'sort by price' handed to a shop assistant.
concepts.why: Lets you customize standard tools like sort and search.

concepts.name: sort
concepts.plain: Putting items in order. std::sort does it if you tell it how to compare two items.
concepts.example: Sorting playing cards by number.
concepts.why: Don't write your own sort; use the standard one.

concepts.name: Aggregation
concepts.plain: Turning many records into summary numbers: totals, counts, averages.
concepts.example: The total at the bottom of your bank statement.
concepts.why: Reports and dashboards are all aggregation.

concepts.name: Research
concepts.plain: Finding out how something works using docs, articles and small experiments.
concepts.example: Reading reviews and comparing before buying a phone.
concepts.why: Nobody knows everything. Developers look things up all day.

concepts.name: Inverted index
concepts.plain: A lookup table from each word to where it appears.
concepts.example: The index at the back of a textbook.
concepts.why: It's how search engines are fast.

concepts.name: Measuring performance
concepts.plain: Timing your code instead of guessing what's slow.
concepts.example: Using a stopwatch instead of 'it feels fast'.
concepts.why: Guesses about speed are often wrong.

concepts.name: Copy vs move
concepts.plain: Copying duplicates data; moving hands it over without duplicating.
concepts.example: Photocopying a box of papers vs just handing over the box.
concepts.why: Moving big data is much faster than copying it.

concepts.name: unordered_map
concepts.plain: Like map, but not sorted and usually faster (uses hashing).
concepts.example: A coat check: ticket number -> coat. Order doesn't matter.
concepts.why: Fastest general lookup when you don't need order.

concepts.name: set
concepts.plain: A collection with no duplicates.
concepts.example: The countries you've visited - each counted once.
concepts.why: Removes duplicates for free and answers 'is X in here?' fast.

concepts.name: Project scope
concepts.plain: Deciding what you WILL and WON'T build.
concepts.example: Planning a 3-day trip: you can't see every city.
concepts.why: Small and finished beats huge and half-done.

items.label: 1. Read (5 min)
items.text: Find your next row in Plan. Read Task, What to do and Done when.

items.label: 2. Learn the words (5 min)
items.text: Any concept in the 'Concepts today' column you don't know? Read it in the Concepts tab. 🆕 marks a concept you're meeting for the first time.

items.label: 3. Look things up (5-10 min)
items.text: Answer the 'Think about' questions. Write short answers or links in Notes.

items.label: 4. Plan (5 min)
items.text: For anything tricky, write pseudocode in Notes before coding (template below).

items.label: 5. Build (20-40 min)
items.text: Do 'What to do'. ⭐ Stretch goals are only for days you have extra time.

items.label: 6. Check (5 min)
items.text: Go through 'Done when'. All true? Set Status to Done and fill in Minutes.

items.label: Not started / In progress
items.text: It's fine for one row to take 2 sessions.

items.label: Stuck
items.text: Stuck for 15+ minutes. Fill in the stuck template (below) in Notes, then ask for help.

items.label: Done
items.text: Everything in 'Done when' is true.

items.label: Level
items.text: ★☆☆☆ easy  ·  ★★☆☆ medium  ·  ★★★☆ hard  ·  ★★★★ challenge (expect 2 sessions)

items.label: Yellow rows
items.text: Checkpoints: catch up, re-check, reflect. On track? Do stretch goals instead.

items.label: 1. Ask good questions
items.text: Before asking for help, answer: What am I trying to do? What have I tried? What's the exact error? What do I think is happening? What did I look up? Can I describe the steps in plain English?

items.label: 2. Research is the work
items.text: Docs, Stack Overflow, articles, AI tools - all allowed. But if you use code from anywhere, you must be able to explain every line. If you can't yet, don't use it yet.

items.label: 3. Pseudocode first
items.text: Problem -> Input -> Expected output -> Steps in plain English -> Code -> Check.

items.label: 4. Test everything
items.text: Use the 7 test types below for every feature.

items.label: 5. Reflect
items.text: Weekly Reflection every week; Project Review after each project.

items.label: Normal
items.text: Typical valid input. Does the basic thing work?

items.label: Invalid
items.text: Wrong values: letters in a number, GPA 5.0, negative age.

items.label: Empty
items.text: Nothing typed. Only spaces. An empty list.

items.label: Missing
items.text: Search, update or delete something that doesn't exist.

items.label: Duplicate
items.text: The same ID twice. The same action twice.

items.label: Boundary
items.text: The exact edges: GPA 0.0 and 4.0, the first and last item.

items.label: Unexpected
items.text: Weird order of actions, very long text, quitting half-way.

items.label: How
items.text: At each checkpoint, copy your whole project folder and name it as the checkpoint says (e.g. StudentManager_V1). Broke something badly? Go back to the copy.

  1. ...
  2. ...
  3. ...

resources.name: learncpp.com
resources.use: Beginner-friendly C++ lessons. Best first stop when a concept is new.

resources.name: cppreference
resources.use: The exact C++ reference. Dense - scroll to the Example at the bottom first.

resources.name: Qt 6 documentation
resources.use: Every Qt class (from week 6). Search the class name and read 'Detailed Description'.

resources.name: Stack Overflow
resources.use: Search your exact error message. Read the question AND the top answers.

resources.name: Project Gutenberg
resources.use: Free text files for the week 10 search engine.

resources.name: AI tools
